ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ninety Western European university students participated in a within-subjects laboratory study in which they discussed the university's current collaborations (status quo condition) followed by implementing an academic boycott-like change targeting unethical institutional collaborations (social change condition).
To confirm that participants are engaged in a task, two physiological markers are typically used: heart rate (HR) and pre-ejection period (PEP).
table.header: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat and Its Relevance to Social Change

table.text: Extending this work, Long et al. (2025) found that political orientation moderated cardiovascular responses in line with the BPS-CT framework: when participants were informed that public support for structural changes benefiting migrants had increased, right-leaning individuals displayed physiological patterns indicative of threat and heightened anti-migrant prejudice, whereas left-leaning individuals showed patterns consistent with challenge, and increased pro-migrant attitudes and resource appraisal.
table.formatted: Extending this work, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Long et al. (2025)</ref> found that political orientation moderated cardiovascular responses in line with the BPS-CT framework: when participants were informed that public support for structural changes benefiting migrants had increased, right-leaning individuals displayed physiological patterns indicative of threat and heightened anti-migrant prejudice, whereas left-leaning individuals showed patterns consistent with challenge, and increased pro-migrant attitudes and resource appraisal.
table.header: Resistance and Physiological Responses to Social Change

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions of level of change.
Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machine and then completed a computer task.
Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change.
Participants were asked to deliver a one-minute speech about their thoughts and feelings regarding the collaboration model that was described in the text they read.
table.header: Speech Task About Social Change and Speech-Coded Demands and Resources

table.text: To explore whether threat and challenge responses influence action intentions, participants were asked at the end of the study to write up to 200 characters describing whether they would take action in relation to the selective collaboration model, and if so, what action.

We additionally examined whether cardiovascular challenge-threat responses varied as a function of the level of change manipulation (i.e., whether participants were instructed to focus their reflection on themselves, their ingroup, or the system) by adding the interaction between state of change and level of change to our previous models predicting CO, TPR, and TCI.

Descriptively, participants were, on average, moderately left-leaning (M = 5.00, SD = 1.18, on a 7-point scale), reported relatively positive eco-justice attitudes (M = 5.01, SD = 1.06), and expressed moderate opposition to neoliberal capitalism (M = 3.52, SD = 0.86).
table.header: Cardiovascular Threat Among Supporters of Change

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Ninety Western European university students participated in a within-subjects laboratory study in which they discussed the university's current collaborations (status quo condition) followed by implementing an academic boycott-like change targeting unethical institutional collaborations (social change condition).

> To confirm that participants are engaged in a task, two physiological markers are typically used: heart rate (HR) and pre-ejection period (PEP).

> Extending this work, Long et al. (2025) found that political orientation moderated cardiovascular responses in line with the BPS-CT framework: when participants were informed that public support for structural changes benefiting migrants had increased, right-leaning individuals displayed physiological patterns indicative of threat and heightened anti-migrant prejudice, whereas left-leaning individuals showed patterns consistent with challenge, and increased pro-migrant attitudes and resource appraisal.

> Participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions of level of change.

> Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machine and then completed a computer task.

> Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change.

> Participants were asked to deliver a one-minute speech about their thoughts and feelings regarding the collaboration model that was described in the text they read.

> To explore whether threat and challenge responses influence action intentions, participants were asked at the end of the study to write up to 200 characters describing whether they would take action in relation to the selective collaboration model, and if so, what action.

> We additionally examined whether cardiovascular challenge-threat responses varied as a function of the level of change manipulation (i.e., whether participants were instructed to focus their reflection on themselves, their ingroup, or the system) by adding the interaction between state of change and level of change to our previous models predicting CO, TPR, and TCI.

> Descriptively, participants were, on average, moderately left-leaning (M = 5.00, SD = 1.18, on a 7-point scale), reported relatively positive eco-justice attitudes (M = 5.01, SD = 1.06), and expressed moderate opposition to neoliberal capitalism (M = 3.52, SD = 0.86).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To determine sample size requirements, we conducted an a-priori power analysis, using G*Power 3.0.10 (Faul et al., 2007) for the within-subject, and within-subject × between-subject interactions. To achieve a power of .90 at α = 0.05, assuming a medium effect size (f = .20), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of 64 participants for the within-subjects effects and 84 participants for the 2 (within-subjects) × 3 (between-subjects) interaction. We collected responses among students at a large West-European university between March and June 2023.

To achieve a power of .90 at α = 0.05, assuming a medium effect size (f = .20), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of 64 participants for the within-subjects effects and 84 participants for the 2 (within-subjects) × 3 (between-subjects) interaction. We collected responses among students at a large West-European university between March and June 2023."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

table.formatted: Mixedmodel effects further revealed that participants expressed stronger support for the academic boycott (M = 5.40, SD = 1.46) than for the status quo (M = 3.19, SD = 1.18), β = 1.35, 95% CI [1.13, 1.58], p < .001.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≥ .18", Text = "Importantly, none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance (all ps ≥ .18), suggesting that the threatening effect of social change also persisted among its supporters."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Put these letter and numbers in a sequence: The last letter of your first name The last letter of your surname Your birth day (day) Your birth month (dd) The first three letter of the city you were born to. For example, if you are Amin a Norman Prat t , born the 17 / 03 /1985, in Val encia, your code is: at1703val . Please use only lower case, and do not put any space. NB: You can note this code down, as we will ask you to use it during your lab session, but you do not need to: The instructions will be repeated during the lab session.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1096 columns across 30 data files.
#### Issues Identified

74 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 30 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Ninety Western European university students participated in a within-subjects laboratory study in which they discussed the university's current collaborations (status quo condition) followed by implementing an academic boycott-like change targeting unethical institutional collaborations (social change condition).
To confirm that participants are engaged in a task, two physiological markers are typically used: heart rate (HR) and pre-ejection period (PEP).

Extending this work, Long et al. (2025) found that political orientation moderated cardiovascular responses in line with the BPS-CT framework: when participants were informed that public support for structural changes benefiting migrants had increased, right-leaning individuals displayed physiological patterns indicative of threat and heightened anti-migrant prejudice, whereas left-leaning individuals showed patterns consistent with challenge, and increased pro-migrant attitudes and resource appraisal.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions of level of change.
Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machine and then completed a computer task.
Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change.
Participants were asked to deliver a one-minute speech about their thoughts and feelings regarding the collaboration model that was described in the text they read.

To explore whether threat and challenge responses influence action intentions, participants were asked at the end of the study to write up to 200 characters describing whether they would take action in relation to the selective collaboration model, and if so, what action.

We additionally examined whether cardiovascular challenge-threat responses varied as a function of the level of change manipulation (i.e., whether participants were instructed to focus their reflection on themselves, their ingroup, or the system) by adding the interaction between state of change and level of change to our previous models predicting CO, TPR, and TCI.

Descriptively, participants were, on average, moderately left-leaning (M = 5.00, SD = 1.18, on a 7-point scale), reported relatively positive eco-justice attitudes (M = 5.01, SD = 1.06), and expressed moderate opposition to neoliberal capitalism (M = 3.52, SD = 0.86).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "speaking progress feeling threat_r script.rmd", 
    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `speaking progress feeling threat_irr.sav`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "speaking progress feeling threat_r script.rmd", 
    Outcome = "errored", Detail = "runtime", "Time (s)" = 4.9), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "speaking progress feeling threat_r script.rmd", 
    "setwd() removed" = 1L, "Path(s) it set" = "C:/Users/Colom009/OneDrive - Universiteit Utrecht/Desktop/work in progress/threat social change/chapter 2"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

28 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. info.title: Speaking Progress, Feeling Threat: A Biopsychosocial Approach to Systemic Progressive Social Change
keywords: collective action Not Only Resistance as Opposition: Resistance Among Supporters of Social Change

text.text: Progressive values are substantially endorsed across Western Europe, yet concrete engagement with social change remains limited.
This gap raises questions about the motivational and physiological processes that may underlie ambivalence toward progressive action.

Drawing on the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT), the present study examined whether progressive hierarchy-disruptive social change elicit cardiovascular threat responses even among individuals who support such change.

Ninety Western European university students participated in a within-subjects laboratory study in which they discussed the university's current collaborations (status quo condition) followed by implementing an academic boycott-like change targeting unethical institutional collaborations (social change condition).
Cardiovascular responses were assessed via cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance (TPR), and the Threat-Challenge Index (TCI), and analyzed using multilevel modeling.
In line with preregistered predictions, the social-change condition elicited stronger physiological threat than the status-quo (lower or stable CO, higher TPR, lower TCI).
These responses persisted after controlling for political orientation and (progressive) attitudes, and despite participants generally expressing high support for social change.
Text analyses revealed heterogeneity in the sources of threat: Participants either showed reluctance to relinquish status-quo privileges or voiced practical concerns regarding the change.
By contrast, relative challenge, which was less prevalent, related to perceiving collective resources to deal with the change but also to rationalization of opposition.
These findings suggest that even supporting individuals are not always immune to threat responses when confronting material systemic change.
Across Western Europe, governments and corporations have increasingly endorsed progressive values by committing to human rights, diversity and inclusion, and sustainability.
At the same time, these same institutions continue to perpetrate structural violence and exploitation.

In particular, despite strong verbal commitments to diversity, only a fraction of European organizations (as low as 7% in 2023) manage to build inclusive cultures (EY, 2024), and economic inequality remains extreme worldwide (World Inequality Lab, 2022).
text.formatted: In particular, despite strong verbal commitments to diversity, only a fraction of European organizations (as low as 7% in 2023) manage to build inclusive cultures <ref type="bibr">(EY, 2024)</ref>, and economic inequality remains extreme worldwide <ref type="bibr">(World Inequality Lab, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Large corporations invest heavily in sustainability branding even as their core operations destroy ecosystems and cause deaths among local populations, a pattern exemplified by Shell's contamination of the Niger Delta and Ogoniland (CODE ROOD, 2020; Amnesty International Nederland, n.d.).

Moreover, governments routinely condemn international human-rights violations while maintaining the political and economic ties that may fuel them, as in the recent case of Europe remaining Israel's largest economic partner, with tens of billions funneling into the ongoing genocide in Gaza (Albanese, 2025; Van Teeffelen, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, governments routinely condemn international human-rights violations while maintaining the political and economic ties that may fuel them, as in the recent case of Europe remaining Israel's largest economic partner, with tens of billions funneling into the ongoing genocide in Gaza <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Albanese, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Teeffelen, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These examples highlight a persistent gap between progressive rhetoric and hierarchydisruptive social change, where with hierarchy-disruptive social change we mean material and systemic social change that aims to dismantle unjust hierarchies, and that is rooted in minoritized communities' objectives and social movements initiatives.
This gap may be reflected in how individuals respond to social change and how they navigate its implications.

Notably, Western European citizens increasingly endorse liberal values (Inglehart et al., 2023), yet translating these values into actions remains uncommon, such as engagement in protests and political boycotts lying below 15% as of 2023 (OECD, 2024).
text.formatted: Notably, Western European citizens increasingly endorse liberal values <ref type="bibr">(Inglehart et al., 2023</ref>), yet translating these values into actions remains uncommon, such as engagement in protests and political boycotts lying below 15% as of 2023 <ref type="bibr">(OECD, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Could these gaps help explain why structural inequalities and violence continue under a veneer of progressivism?

Physiological and psychological threat and resistance to social change have been found particularly among dominant-group members (Knowles et al., 2014; Scheepers & Knight, 2020) and conservatives (Long et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Physiological and psychological threat and resistance to social change have been found particularly among dominant-group members <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Knowles et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Scheepers & Knight, 2020)</ref> and conservatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Long et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging work also showed that supporters of progressive causes can exhibit ambivalence or hesitation toward collective action (e.g., Kutlaca & Radke, 2022; Uysal et al., 2025), hinting at deeper motivational tensions between the ideals and realities of progress.
text.formatted: Emerging work also showed that supporters of progressive causes can exhibit ambivalence or hesitation toward collective action (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Kutlaca & Radke, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Uysal et al., 2025)</ref>, hinting at deeper motivational tensions between the ideals and realities of progress.

text.text: Taken together, these findings raise the question of whether physiological threat (potentially driven by demand appraisals concerning status loss, uncertainty about the stakes, or fear of failure) may help explain the ambivalence or hesitation sometimes observed among progressive individuals in collective action and attitudeimplementation gap research.

The present study introduces a novel approach to understanding these complexities by combining cardiovascular measures from the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996) with analyses of how individuals verbally reflect their stance on hierarchy-disruptive social change (an academic boycott-like initiative).
text.formatted: The present study introduces a novel approach to understanding these complexities by combining cardiovascular measures from the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996)</ref> with analyses of how individuals verbally reflect their stance on hierarchy-disruptive social change (an academic boycott-like initiative).

text.text: We experimentally tested whether expressing one's opinion about social change elicited cardiovascular threat responses, and whether these responses persisted beyond professed progressivism, operationalized through political orientation and both survey-based and speechcoded attitudes toward the political issues at hand.
We then tested whether survey-based demands and resources predicted physiological threat and challenge responses.

Next, we examined potential sources of threat and challenge by clustering participants based on the speech-coded support, demands, and resources of social change, and examining physiological differences across these clusters.

Finally, we explored whether threat and challenge responses, as well as speech-coded support of social change, influenced participants' action intentions, as assessed through responses to a short open-ended question.
A possible explanation for the gap between ideals and action is symbolic or performative behavior.

Performative allyship refers to low-cost, sometimes visible actions, such as social media posts or attending events, that signal support for marginalized groups without necessarily challenging structural inequality (Kutlaca & Radke, 2022).
text.formatted: Performative allyship refers to low-cost, sometimes visible actions, such as social media posts or attending events, that signal support for marginalized groups without necessarily challenging structural inequality <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kutlaca & Radke, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such gestures often function as virtue signaling or identity reinforcement, serving personal and ingroup needs more than social change.

Kutlaca and Radke also argue that self-serving motifs may coexist with more progressive ones (i.e., genuine care for minority well-being and causes), creating a more complex picture for supporters of progress.
Other work emphasized more situational and psychological constraints that can limit action.

For instance, Uysal et al. (2025) found that individuals' engagement in confrontational collective actions, defined as more disruptive and costly, is influenced by perceptions of the legitimacy and the efficacy of the tactic deployed.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr">Uysal et al. (2025)</ref> found that individuals' engagement in confrontational collective actions, defined as more disruptive and costly, is influenced by perceptions of the legitimacy and the efficacy of the tactic deployed.

text.text: Furthermore, while moral obligation more strongly motivates action, both the subjective importance of potential risks (e.g., arrest, police brutality) and, to a lesser extent, the perceived likelihood of those risks slightly influenced participation in context-dependent ways: Individuals with high moral commitment may still act under high-risk conditions, but when risks are judged as highly important or threatening, they can somewhat inhibit participation (Uysal et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Furthermore, while moral obligation more strongly motivates action, both the subjective importance of potential risks (e.g., arrest, police brutality) and, to a lesser extent, the perceived likelihood of those risks slightly influenced participation in context-dependent ways: Individuals with high moral commitment may still act under high-risk conditions, but when risks are judged as highly important or threatening, they can somewhat inhibit participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Uysal et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This body of work has been invaluable in highlighting the complex ambivalences that can accompany progressive attitudes.
Building on these insights, an important next step is to examine the processes that may underlie these gaps.
Beside Long et al. (2025), no study has directly examined physiological threat responses to social change as a function of support and opposition, be it ideological or attitudinal.
text.formatted: Beside <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Long et al. (2025)</ref>, no study has directly examined physiological threat responses to social change as a function of support and opposition, be it ideological or attitudinal.

text.text: This leaves open the questions of whether support for social change can coexist with physiological threat, and how people experience and navigate such conflicting states (see Dixon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This leaves open the questions of whether support for social change can coexist with physiological threat, and how people experience and navigate such conflicting states (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Dixon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: To investigate such processes, we deemed it appropriate to use an approach that can detect implicit, momentary reactions, namely the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT).

The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT) was developed to assess motivational stress states along a continuum from challenge to threat through cardiovascular (CV) reactivity during motivated performance situations: Contexts in which individuals are evaluated while pursuing a goal, such as taking a test or formulating and expressing one's opinion on a certain topic (Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996).
text.formatted: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT) was developed to assess motivational stress states along a continuum from challenge to threat through cardiovascular (CV) reactivity during motivated performance situations: Contexts in which individuals are evaluated while pursuing a goal, such as taking a test or formulating and expressing one's opinion on a certain topic <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Blascovich & Tomaka, 1996)</ref>.

text.text: Challenge reflects a more adaptive form of stress, whereas threat reflects a more maladaptive form of stress.

In the present study, this type of motivated performance situation took the form of giving a speech, in which participants reflected on and expressed their views regarding systemic progressive social change.

Although less confrontational than many political actions (e.g., Uysal et al., 2025), giving a speech functioned as a modest political act (Arsith, 2015) and reflected the common daily practice of sharing opinions and engaging in political reflection.
text.formatted: Although less confrontational than many political actions (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Uysal et al., 2025)</ref>, giving a speech functioned as a modest political act <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arsith, 2015)</ref> and reflected the common daily practice of sharing opinions and engaging in political reflection.

text.text: It thus provided a meaningful and reproducible laboratory context for observing the motivational conflicts underlying threat and challenge responses.
According to the BPS-CT, task engagement is a prerequisite for both challenge and threat motivational states as it forms an indispensable aspect of motivated performance.
To confirm that participants are engaged in a task, two physiological markers are typically used: heart rate (HR) and pre-ejection period (PEP).
HR reflects the speed of cardiac activity, while PEP is a measure of how forcefully the heart contracts, with lower levels indicating stronger ventricular force.
Task-engagement is inferred when HR increases, and PEP decreases from baseline.
Once engaged, whether more challenge or threat is experienced depends on how individuals appraise the demands of the situation relative to their perceived resources to cope with them.
A challenge state arises when resources (e.g., skills, support, confidence) are perceived to outweigh or meet the demands (e.g., difficulty, stakes, uncertainty).
Conversely, a threat state occurs when demands are seen as exceeding available resources.
Threat and challenge are reflected in distinct cardiovascular (CV) patterns.

In the literature, both absolute and relative patterns of challenge and threat have been described, with relative patterns referring to individuals' baseline responses subtracted from experimental conditions (see Blascovich et al., 2001).
text.formatted: In the literature, both absolute and relative patterns of challenge and threat have been described, with relative patterns referring to individuals' baseline responses subtracted from experimental conditions (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Blascovich et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: More specifically, in absolute terms, compared to baseline, challenge is characterized by increased cardiac output (CO; the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute) and decreased total peripheral resistance (TPR; resistance to blood flow in the vascular system).
In contrast, threat is marked by stable CO and increased TPR, reflecting a more strained and inefficient physiological state.
In relative terms, threat is marked by relatively stable or low CO and high TPR and challenge is marked by relatively high CO and low TPR.
As an elaboration of this relative approach to examining challenge and threat, CO and TPR are typically combined in a single threat-challenge index (TCI; Blascovich et al., 2004).
text.formatted: As an elaboration of this relative approach to examining challenge and threat, CO and TPR are typically combined in a single threat-challenge index (TCI; <ref type="bibr">Blascovich et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: In keeping with current conventions, here we primarily focus on relative patterns of challenge and threat, although we also report the absolute patterns in the https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 5) for the sake of completeness and transparency.

text.text: Importantly, challenge and threat have distinct implications: threat is linked to generally poorer performance, health, and well-being, whereas challenge relates to more adaptive outcomes (Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: Importantly, challenge and threat have distinct implications: threat is linked to generally poorer performance, health, and well-being, whereas challenge relates to more adaptive outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Although both states involve heightened cardiovascular reactivity and cognitive engagement, threat is marked by avoidance and defensiveness whereas challenge tends to facilitate more open, approach-oriented behavior (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: Although both states involve heightened cardiovascular reactivity and cognitive engagement, threat is marked by avoidance and defensiveness whereas challenge tends to facilitate more open, approach-oriented behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These distinctions may be relevant in the context of social change, where avoidance and withdrawal associated with threat may help explain the attitudinal and behavioral divergences described in the principle-implementation gap and collective-action research.

Moreover, challenge states are more commonly associated with anger, an emotion found to promote collective action, whereas threat states are linked to fear and guilt, emotions that typically dampen participation and reinforce resistance (Miller et al., 2017; Blascovich & Mendes, 2010).
text.formatted: Moreover, challenge states are more commonly associated with anger, an emotion found to promote collective action, whereas threat states are linked to fear and guilt, emotions that typically dampen participation and reinforce resistance <ref type="bibr">(Miller et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, it is plausible that some supporters of progressive causes experience social change as threatening rather than challenging.
Such threat responses could partly account for why support does not always translate into advocacy and participation.

Framing these responses within a stress-and-coping framework, and as dynamic rather than fixed traits, may also open possibilities for fostering more adaptive, challenge-oriented appraisals of social change.

To date, however, physiological research has primarily focused on threat responses in relation to opposition to social change (Domen et al., 2022), leaving these dynamics among supporters comparatively understudied.
text.formatted: To date, however, physiological research has primarily focused on threat responses in relation to opposition to social change <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Domen et al., 2022)</ref>, leaving these dynamics among supporters comparatively understudied.

text.text: Psychological and physiological research has provided valuable insight into how social change can elicit threat, often linking opposition and resistance to higher status and conservative orientations.

For example, studies grounded in the BPS-CT showed that when social hierarchies become unstable, lower-status individuals tend to exhibit challenge responses, perceiving opportunities in change, whereas higher-status individuals often show threat responses, perceiving risks to their position (Scheepers & Knight, 2020; Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018).
text.formatted: For example, studies grounded in the BPS-CT showed that when social hierarchies become unstable, lower-status individuals tend to exhibit challenge responses, perceiving opportunities in change, whereas higher-status individuals often show threat responses, perceiving risks to their position <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Scheepers & Knight, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, hinting at the pattern of tensions mentioned above, Scheepers et al. (2009) found that men displayed physiological signs of threat when discussing progressive gender roles with a woman (but not with another man), yet simultaneously expressed low sexism and support for affirmative action.
text.formatted: Interestingly, hinting at the pattern of tensions mentioned above, <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Scheepers et al. (2009)</ref> found that men displayed physiological signs of threat when discussing progressive gender roles with a woman (but not with another man), yet simultaneously expressed low sexism and support for affirmative action.

text.text: Extending this work, Long et al. (2025) found that political orientation moderated cardiovascular responses in line with the BPS-CT framework: when participants were informed that public support for structural changes benefiting migrants had increased, right-leaning individuals displayed physiological patterns indicative of threat and heightened anti-migrant prejudice, whereas left-leaning individuals showed patterns consistent with challenge, and increased pro-migrant attitudes and resource appraisal.

(2025)</ref> found that political orientation moderated cardiovascular responses in line with the BPS-CT framework: when participants were informed that public support for structural changes benefiting migrants had increased, right-leaning individuals displayed physiological patterns indicative of threat and heightened anti-migrant prejudice, whereas left-leaning individuals showed patterns consistent with challenge, and increased pro-migrant attitudes and resource appraisal.

text.text: When taking a close look at how previous research has conceptualized and operationalized social change, one would notice that much of this work has focused on relatively abstract operationalizations and centered intergroup dynamics, such as controlled intergroup encounters, shifts in public opinion, or group competitions, providing solid insight into how dominant groups and conservatives often experience threat and resistance as they fear to lose status and power.

Additionally, the consistent challenge responses observed among leftleaning participants could be partially explained by the design of previous research inadvertently reinforcing resource appraisal through ingroup values and identity reinforcement (e.g., progressive shifts in public opinion might be perceived as support or moral validation by left-leaning individuals).
How might these dynamics play out if progressive individuals were confronted with the more complex, politicized realities of hierarchy-disruptive social change (see Pratto & Stewart, 2020)?
text.formatted: How might these dynamics play out if progressive individuals were confronted with the more complex, politicized realities of hierarchy-disruptive social change (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Pratto & Stewart, 2020)</ref>?

text.text: With this consideration, our study conceptualized hierarchy-disruptive social change as systemic and material, rooted in the objectives of minoritized communities and informed by real-world social movements, including academic boycotts (CODE ROOD, n.d.
; PACBI, n.d.), with the primary aim of dismantling unjust hierarchies.

We then operationalized social change as a reading and speech task in which participants first read about an academic boycott-like scenario possibly being implemented soon, and then articulated their opinions about this change.
This design aligned with BPS-CT assumptions (i.e., high-stakes motivated performance).

Furthermore, political boycotts have a long and effective history within social movements, from their role in the anti-apartheid struggle for South Africa, to their influence on climate-justice, and the current mobilizations for Palestinian rights, as documented by Barghouti (2011), and Ayling and Gunningham (2017).
text.formatted: Furthermore, political boycotts have a long and effective history within social movements, from their role in the anti-apartheid struggle for South Africa, to their influence on climate-justice, and the current mobilizations for Palestinian rights, as documented by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Barghouti (2011)</ref>, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Ayling and Gunningham (2017)</ref>.

text.text: By situating the task within this historically grounded and politically meaningful tradition, the project responds to researchers' calls for more context-sensitive and qualitatively informed approaches (see Dixon et al., 2017), while connecting the research to ongoing political struggles.
text.formatted: By situating the task within this historically grounded and politically meaningful tradition, the project responds to researchers' calls for more context-sensitive and qualitatively informed approaches (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Dixon et al., 2017)</ref>, while connecting the research to ongoing political struggles.

text.text: Hierarchy-disruptive social change involves shifts in formal structures, social norms, power relations, and collective expectations, generating multiple sources of uncertainty and instability (Pratto & Stewart, 2020; de la Sablonnière, 2017).
text.formatted: Hierarchy-disruptive social change involves shifts in formal structures, social norms, power relations, and collective expectations, generating multiple sources of uncertainty and instability <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Pratto & Stewart, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">de la Sablonnière, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These changes are particularly challenging when centering the objectives and strategies of minoritized communities, as they disrupt hegemonic scripts and raise the stakes for both dominant and marginalized individuals (Garay & Remedios, 2021; Lorde, 1979; Freire, 1970).
text.formatted: These changes are particularly challenging when centering the objectives and strategies of minoritized communities, as they disrupt hegemonic scripts and raise the stakes for both dominant and marginalized individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Garay & Remedios, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lorde, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Freire, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: According to the BPS-CT, uncertainty is central to demanding situations (Blascovich, 2008; Seery, 2013), potentially making systemic progressive change difficult to navigate, even for supporters.
text.formatted: According to the BPS-CT, uncertainty is central to demanding situations <ref type="bibr">(Blascovich, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery, 2013)</ref>, potentially making systemic progressive change difficult to navigate, even for supporters.

text.text: When articulating their views, individuals must contend with uncertainties and social evaluation.
People are especially sensitive to moral scrutiny, showing threat responses when their actions are perceived as violating norms or confronted by a moral refuser (Cramwinckel et al., 2013).
text.formatted: People are especially sensitive to moral scrutiny, showing threat responses when their actions are perceived as violating norms or confronted by a moral refuser <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Cramwinckel et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Progressive individuals may experience heightened moral demands due to their sensitivity to fairness (Stewart & Morris, 2021).
text.formatted: Progressive individuals may experience heightened moral demands due to their sensitivity to fairness <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Stewart & Morris, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Social change also has a prefigurative dimension: Individuals face the difficulty of translating ideas of progress into tangible practices, institutions, and social relations (Komporozos-Athanasiou & Bottici, 2022).
text.formatted: Social change also has a prefigurative dimension: Individuals face the difficulty of translating ideas of progress into tangible practices, institutions, and social relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Komporozos-Athanasiou & Bottici, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This can expose them to potential losses, unfamiliar routines, and risks of implementing and sustaining change.
Despite these demands, individuals can draw on resources to navigate them.

For example, moral obligation strongly motivates engagement in collective action, suggesting that progressive individuals may rely on their moral commitments to persist despite risk or loss (Uysal et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, moral obligation strongly motivates engagement in collective action, suggesting that progressive individuals may rely on their moral commitments to persist despite risk or loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Uysal et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In line with the BPS-CT, strategies such as reappraising arousal, positive self-talk, or recalling past successes can further promote challenge responses (Hase, 2025).
text.formatted: In line with the BPS-CT, strategies such as reappraising arousal, positive self-talk, or recalling past successes can further promote challenge responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hase, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, people may also draw from collective resources such as support networks, perceived group cohesion, and collective efficacy, i.e., the often-shared belief that one's group can effect change, which can all bolster engagement and persistence in social movements (Bandura, 2000; Li et al., 2022; Uysal, 2025).
text.formatted: Finally, people may also draw from collective resources such as support networks, perceived group cohesion, and collective efficacy, i.e., the often-shared belief that one's group can effect change, which can all bolster engagement and persistence in social movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bandura, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Li et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Uysal, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, given the unprecedented and drastic nature of hierarchy-disruptive social change (see de la Sablonnière, 2017), such resources may be, at least initially, difficult to access or unevenly distributed, particularly in contexts such as the Netherlands and Europe more broadly, where increasing neoliberal individualization and the fragmentation of organized political and supportive networks may constrain opportunities for collective support and mobilization.
Thus, we expected individuals to perceive heightened demands and depleted resources in relation to social change, compared to the status quo.
In the present study, we examined these potential demands and related resources using both surveybased and speech-coded measures, and their effect on physiological responses.

Building on psychological evidence of a gap between progressive ideals and behavior, as well as physiological evidence of threat responses to social change, the present study examined whether expressing one's opinion about a hierarchy-disruptive social change elicited cardiovascular threat responses, even among its supporters.
The social change under examination was an academic boycott-like initiative.

We developed such experimental manipulation with inspiration from contemporary social movements, specifically the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) campaign (Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel [PACBI], n.d.) and the Shell Must Fall campaign (CODE ROOD, n.d.).

The real-world relevance of this topic was particularly salient because data collection took place just weeks before campus protests and occupations in which students demanded that the university implement an academic boycott targeting both the fossil fuel industry and Israeli academic institutions.
Participants' physiological responses were assessed alongside political orientation and attitudes toward change, measured through both survey and speech coding.
We further analyzed survey-and speech-based indicators of demands and resources to explore how individuals navigate conflicting motivations underlying support (and opposition) to change.
We identified clusters based on speech-coded attitude, demands, and resources about social change and examined their differences in physiological threat and challenge responses.

We included this qualitative component in line with Dixon et al. (2017), who argue that qualitative data are essential for understanding how individuals make sense of and navigate policy-related "political dilemmas," particularly when personal principles and behavioral implications are in tension.
text.formatted: We included this qualitative component in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Dixon et al. (2017)</ref>, who argue that qualitative data are essential for understanding how individuals make sense of and navigate policy-related "political dilemmas," particularly when personal principles and behavioral implications are in tension.

text.text: From their perspective, policy attitudes are not treated as direct reflections of stable internal beliefs, but as situated, action-oriented accounts through which individuals justify and negotiate potentially conflicting motivations, which are more difficult to measure using survey measures.
Finally, we explored the effects of threat and challenge responses, and speech-coded support on action intentions, via a short open question.

Our preregistered hypotheses were as follows: (1) Compared to maintaining the status quo, social change elicits stronger threat responses, even when accounting for political orientation and attitudes toward change; (2) this effect is mediated by the extent to which perceived demands outweigh available resources.

Our exploratory preregistered analyses focused on: (1) the qualitative content of speech-coded demands and resources; (2) whether expressed support and threat and challenge responses influence action intentions.

Given the multidimensionality of demands, resources, and social change itself, we also explored whether framing one's speech at the personal, ingroup, or systemic level would influence threat and challenge responses.
To test this, we included a between-subject manipulation of speech focus (level of change).
However, this manipulation did not function as intended; therefore, this factor was not included in the following analyses.
Full methodological details and results regarding this manipulation are reported in https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 7).

text.text: To determine sample size requirements, we conducted an a-priori power analysis, using G*Power 3.0.10 (Faul et al., 2007) for the within-subject, and within-subject × between-subject interactions.
text.formatted: To determine sample size requirements, we conducted an a-priori power analysis, using G*Power 3.0.10 <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Faul et al., 2007)</ref> for the within-subject, and within-subject × between-subject interactions.

text.text: To achieve a power of .90 at α = 0.05, assuming a medium effect size (f = .20), the analysis indicated a minimum sample size of 64 participants for the within-subjects effects and 84 participants for the 2 (within-subjects) × 3 (between-subjects) interaction.
We collected responses among students at a large West-European university between March and June 2023.
Ultimately, 90 cases with valid data were collected.
We paid participants €12,00.
The sample's political orientation was slightly skewed toward the left (M = 5.00 on a 7-point scale, with 'extreme right' and 'extreme left' as endpoints; SD = 1.18; Sk = -.71).
The average age of the final sample was 22 years old (SD = 3.14).

The majority of participant came from western (n = 61; 67,8%) and eastern (n = 10; 11.1%) Europe, followed by east Asia (n = 5; 5.6%), South Africa (n = 3; 3.3%), Caribbean (n = 2; 2.2%), Latin America (n = 2; 2,2%), the Middle-east (n = 2; 2.2%), South Asia (n = 2; 2.2%), North America (n=2; 2,2%), and Southeast Asia (n=1; 1.1%).
Regarding minority status, 27 people identified as BIPoC, 33 as LGBTQ+, 63 as women, and 28 as working class or low middle class.
The sample's average (family) income was between €50,000 and €80,000 (M = 3.55, SD = 1.70) and slightly skewed toward lower incomes.
We used a 2 (state of change: status quo; social change) x 3 (level of change: system; ingroup; personal) mixed design with repeated measures on the first factor.

State of change was not randomized for theoretical and ecological reasons, as social change is typically interpreted relative to a stable status quo (de la Sablonnière, 2017), suggesting that the status quo condition should be presented first to establish a common reference point across participants and minimize variability due to differences in prior knowledge of the social change topic.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the three conditions of level of change.
However, as aforementioned, level of change was left out from following analyses.
Participants first completed a 10-minute online survey in their own time, measuring political orientation, their attitudes towards eco-justice, and neoliberal capitalism.

The online survey closed with demographic questions regarding age, nationality, ethnicity, sex assigned at birth, gender identity, sexual orientation, income, socioeconomic class identity, mental and physical disability, and faculty of study.
Between 24 and 48 hours after completing the survey, participants attended their scheduled laboratory session, which was conducted in the psychophysiology lab at the Science Park of the university.
Participants were connected to the ECG, ICG, and blood pressure machine and then completed a computer task.
During the task, participants first read about the status quo scenario.
They then delivered a one-minute speech about their personal opinion on the reading, which was recorded via a microphone.
The speech was followed by a manipulation check, and the threat and challenge appraisal scales (see below).
This procedure was then repeated a second time for the social change condition.
Complete materials and scoring procedures are available in OSF (https://osf.io/yxvd3/overview?view_only=25061cf09f5449899da4b39515994ce8).

For survey questionnaires, thorough factor analyses were   conducted and are reported in Supplementary Materials Chapter 3</ref> (section 2).

text.text: Participants were presented with a text describing the status quo, followed by a text describing the social change.

We opted for a topic of social change that was relevant for students at our university at the time, while being novel enough to reduce differences in prior knowledge effects: Collaborations between Dutch Academia and external stakeholders.
In the status quo condition, participants read about the "open collaboration model," and in the social change condition participants read about the "selective collaboration model".
While these names were created for the purposes of the study, we designed both scenarios to closely reflect real-world practices.

The open collaboration model reflected the university's current approach, which emphasizes partnerships with a wide range of external entities: A strategy the university promotes on its official website.
In contrast, the selective collaboration Instability, disruption, and novelty are considered main characteristics of social change (de la Sablonnière, 2017).

Thus, in the status quo condition, the social relations between the groups involved (i.e., students, academia, external parties) were described as stable ("This has been the case for a very long time, as Dutch academia follows the 'Open collaboration model'") and long-standing yet impactful ("These long-standing collaborations have a big impact on the university").

In the social change condition, we introduced a disruption of the normative structure of Dutch academia ("They [changing collaboration model] will contribute to reshape finances, quality, characteristics, moral value, and amount of opportunities seen today in the university education and research"), as well as a somewhat rapid pace of change ("According to different sources, it is very likely that change is about to happen at this university and Dutch academia").

Change was framed as unstable ("These changing collaborations are expected to have a very big impact at Utrecht university") and unprecedented ("This is unprecedented for Dutch academia, and it will fall under the new 'selective collaboration model").
Finally, we included real-world examples of collaborations involving parties such as NGOs, Shell, Unilever, KPMG, and ABN Amro.

This aimed to enhance the ecological validity of our manipulation while highlighting the complexity of the issue, which involved both benefits (e.g., job opportunities) and controversies (e.g., workers' rights violations).
Additionally, tailoring the content to the participants, the texts emphasized activities crucial to students, such as "securing internship opportunities," and "setting-up study programs".
By providing this context, we ensured that individuals could form a more informed opinion based on a rounded understanding of the topic.

We evaluated the effectiveness of our manipulation of state of change through a single item, asking participant to rate whether the text they read suggested that "…drastic changes were about to take place in the Netherlands."
This approach, while abstract, was chosen so that the measure could be applied consistently across all three experimental conditions.
We assessed cardiovascular markers for engagement, threat and challenge responses based on established physiological markers (see Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: We assessed cardiovascular markers for engagement, threat and challenge responses based on established physiological markers (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The protocols for physiological data collection and scoring can be found here: https://osf.io/k5gjq/.
text.formatted: The protocols for physiological data collection and scoring can be found here: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/k5gjq/">https://osf.io/k5gjq/</ref>.

text.text: Engagement reflects the degree of sympathetic nervous system activation, indicated by increases in heart rate (HR) and decreases in pre-ejection period (PEP).

Pre-ejection period is a measure of ventricular contractility (VC) and represents the interval between the start of the electromechanical systole (as indicated by the Q-point in the ECG) and the opening of the aorta valve (as indicated by the B-point in the ICG).
Once engaged, individuals may exhibit a challenge or threat cardiovascular profile.
Challenge responses are characterized by relatively high cardiac output (CO) and low total peripheral resistance (TPR), reflecting efficient heart function and vasodilation.
In contrast, threat responses involve relatively low or stable CO combined with relatively high TPR, indicating vasoconstriction and reduced cardiac efficiency.

To capture these physiological responses, we continuously recorded impedance cardiography (ICG), electrocardiography (ECG), and blood pressure (BP) throughout the entire lab session using a Biopac MP150 system (Biopac Systems Inc., Goleta, CA).
To ensure the quality of the physiological data, two experimenters supervised each lab session.
Impedance cardiography is a noninvasive technique for measuring stroke volume (SV) and systolic time intervals (e.g., pre-ejection period; PEP, see Sherwood et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Impedance cardiography is a noninvasive technique for measuring stroke volume (SV) and systolic time intervals (e.g., pre-ejection period; PEP, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sherwood et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Stroke volume, which was determined here using the Kubicek formula (see Sherwood et al., 1990), represents the amount of blood that the heart pumps in one heartbeat.
text.formatted: Stroke volume, which was determined here using the Kubicek formula (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sherwood et al., 1990)</ref>, represents the amount of blood that the heart pumps in one heartbeat.

text.text: Multiplying SV with heart rate (derived from the ECG) yields Cardiac Output (CO; i.e., the amount of blood in liters that the heart pumps per minute).
To measure ICG, we used the Biopac NICO100c module and four spot-electrodes, two of which were placed at the back of the neck, and two on the back, 30cm apart from each other.
The two outer electrodes inject a small (400μA) alternating current while the two inner electrodes measure the voltage developed through the thorax volume.

As output the NICO100c provides measures of baseline impedance (Z0) and the rate of change in impedance (dZ/dt), which can be used to derive measures of cardiac performance (stroke volume, pre-ejection period; see Sherwood et al., 1990).
text.formatted: As output the NICO100c provides measures of baseline impedance (Z0) and the rate of change in impedance (dZ/dt), which can be used to derive measures of cardiac performance (stroke volume, pre-ejection period; see <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Sherwood et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: To measure electrocardiography, we used the ECG100 module and a Lead I electrode configuration (one electrode at the base of the throat, another one four fingers above the last left rib).
To measure blood pressure, we used the NIBP100d module, which is equipped with a finger cuff placed over the index and middle fingers of the non-dominant hand to measure the pulse wave.
The NIBP100d provides a measure of mean arterial pressure (MAP), which, in combination with CO, is used to calculate TPR using the formula: TPR = (MAP/CO) × 80.

For one participant, CV measures could not be accurately calculated due to electrode detachment during the experimental session and were therefore excluded from analyses pertaining to physiological measures.
Physiological data was stored using Acqknowledge (Version 5.0.8.1; BIOPAC Systems, Inc., 2023) and scored using the PhysioData Toolbox (Sjak-Shie, 2022).
For analysis, cardiovascular data were segmented the final minute of the 5-minute baseline period (during which participant watched a relaxing video) and the two 1-minute speech task periods.
The physiological data were manually cleaned, scored, and examined for influential cases by two independent coders, who then met to resolve any major discrepancies.
Following the reactivity approach, we calculated difference scores by subtracting baseline values from task period values.
These difference scores served as the variables in our statistical models.

Finally, we calculated a unified Threat and Challenge Index (TCI) by adding the standardized cardiac output (CO) scores to the inverted standardized total peripheral resistance (TPR) scores (i.e., TPR z-scores multiplied by -1), such that higher values reflect a greater challenge response, and lower values reflect a greater threat response.

In addition to this relative cardiovascular reactivity approach (which is the current standard in research on the BPS-CT), in the https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd section 7).
text.formatted: In addition to this relative cardiovascular reactivity approach (which is the current standard in research on the BPS-CT), in the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd">Supplementary Materials Chapter 3 (section 4) we   also report an analysis of absolute patterns of cardiovascular challenge and threat, as well as   baseline differences across the between-subjects conditions representing levels of change (see   Supplementary Materials Chapter 3,</ref> section 7).

text.text: Participants were asked to deliver a one-minute speech about their thoughts and feelings regarding the collaboration model that was described in the text they read.
The guiding question invited them to focus on the possible consequences of the collaboration model.
Their speeches were automatically transcribed using AmberScript, and then manually coded along the following dimensions, using NVivo (version 14; Lumivero, 2023) and Microsoft Excel.
Speech Coding of Support.

Using a scale from 1 ("Very non-supportive") to 7 ("Very supportive"), we coded the extent to which participants supported the open collaboration model in the status quo condition, and the selective collaboration model in the social change condition.

A score of 1 indicated clear opposition, 2 indicated strong opposition while acknowledging some positive aspects, 3 indicated moderate opposition or reservations, 4 indicated neither support nor opposition, 5 indicated moderate support while expressing some doubts or reservations, 6 indicated strong support with minor reservations, and 7 indicated unequivocal support.
As coding progressed, we further refined the operational criteria used to distinguish between categories.
In particular, we distinguished between general evaluations of the model (e.g., describing it as "good" or "bad") and explicit expressions of support for its implementation.
Explicit statements endorsing implementation were given greater weight because they more directly captured participants' support for the proposed model.
For example, statements such as "I support this" or "I fully support this" were coded as stronger evidence of support than general positive evaluations of the model.
Two independent coders analyzed participants' speeches using iterative thematic coding.

Our approach was grounded in the appraisal component of the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (Blascovich & Mendes, 2000) and followed reflexive thematic analysis guidelines (Braun & Clarke, 2008).

text.text: The aim was to identify perceived demands and resources in participants' views on social change, with demands referring to obstacles, risks, or pressures, and resources reflecting assets, support, or capabilities that help individuals cope with or succeed in implementing the selective collaboration model.
The first coder identified key types of demands and resources using a combination of bottom-up coding and theoretical guidance.
Each speech was reviewed to label segments reflecting these categories, and constant comparison techniques were used to group similar codes into broader themes.
Participants worried about losing personal and ingroup privileges such as funding, internships, and opportunities tied to the current system.

"These collaborations, if they end, they will have effect on all of us because first of all, we will get probably less internship opportunities, less fundings, maybe the tuition fees are going to be higher because the university itself gets less fundings."
Value-interest conflict (34)
Participants experienced tension between endorsing (vague) progressive ideals and managing the practical consequences of the academic boycott.
"Whilst I support civility and definitely hate the actions of big companies like ABN AMRO, I am a bit nervous and afraid to see how this will affect the curriculum of several studies."

The final coding framework comprised three main demands (implementation concerns, status loss, value-interest conflict) and four main resources (moral compass, instrumental support, moral support, rationalizations) (see Tables 1 and 2).
text.formatted: The final coding framework comprised three main demands (implementation concerns, status loss, value-interest conflict) and four main resources (moral compass, instrumental support, moral support, rationalizations) (see Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: After finalizing the coding framework, two coders independently coded the speeches, counting the instances in which each demand and resource were mentioned by participants.
For each coded category of demands and resources, the count per participant generally ranged from 0 to 5.
Moral compass (167)
Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by viewing it as morally necessary and urgent, focusing on longterm benefits despite the sacrifices involved.
"But we all have to make, like, sacrifices.
We all have to do."
Instrumental support ( 23)

text.text: Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by relying on institutional and community practical support.
"I think that's easily manageable for the university if these changes are planned properly in time and not just improvised."
Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by drawing on the collective's ethical leadership and shared community values, emphasizing collective responsibility toward change.
"So I think they should do everything they can […], because everyone in the Western world, everyone in the world has a part to play in that."

text.text: Rationalizations (20)
Participants coped with the demands of the academic boycott by employing various rationalizations, heuristics, and cognitive biases to explain their reluctance toward change.
"So I think collaboration should continue, but some restrictions should be there.
I'm not saying that no restriction at all, but they should continue collaborating."
We finally assessed interrater reliability for the seven coded demands and resources using a two-way random-effects model with absolute agreement intraclass correlation.
The ICCs ranged from .70 to .97 (all ps < .001), indicating good to excellent reliability across codes (ten Hove et al., 2024).
