text.text: Participants self-reported how they appraised the demands and resources associated with each collaboration model.

To assess demands (α = .65 for status quo; α = .60 for social change), we used in total six items capturing perceived effort and uncertainty across three To assess resources (α = .60 for status quo; α = .71 for social change), a total of six items measured perceived ability and support at the same levels.

For instance: "I feel that I can deal with the existence of the 'open collaboration model' at the university" (personal ability), and "I feel that Dutch academia will receive support to deal with the introduction of the 'selective collaboration model'" (system-level support).
Scores for the demands and resources scales were calculated separately by averaging the items within each scale.
Higher values indicated greater demands and greater resources, respectively.
We measure political orientation using a single 7-point Likert scale item, where one endpoint indicated 'far right' and the other 'far left'.

We selected attitude measures that were theoretically linked to our manipulation of social change, thus focusing on sustainability, human rights, and neoliberalism, to further test whether threat persists among supporters of change.
Attitudes toward eco-justice and sustainability were measured using six items developed ad hoc for this study.

The scale captured concerns about natural resource consumption ("In the Netherlands, too little attention is paid to how many natural resources we consume") and CO₂ emissions ("Dutch society has reached the point where CO₂ emissions are under control"; reverse-coded), as well as about climate racism and eco-colonialism ("The Netherlands should teach developing countries how to become more sustainable"; reversecoded).
For analyses, we used the overall mean score across all six items (α = .80), reflecting general ecojustice attitudes.
Neoliberalism.
Attitudes toward neoliberalism were measured using 11 items developed ad hoc for this study.

The scale reflected aspects related to redistribution and public ownership ("In the Netherlands, basic services such as health care and public transport should be public and provided to everyone, free of charge"), and others related to free-market principles, such as competition and private ownership ("Competition in the Dutch economy is good because it stimulates innovation"; reverse-coded).
For analyses, we used the overall mean score across all 10 items (α = .79), reflecting general opposition to neoliberal capitalism.

To explore whether threat and challenge responses influence action intentions, participants were asked at the end of the study to write up to 200 characters describing whether they would take action in relation to the selective collaboration model, and if so, what action.
We opted for this measure due to time constraints and to gain initial insight into how participants spontaneously conceive action in relation to progressive social change.

These brief responses were subsequently coded on a five-point ordinal scale, where 1 indicated no action (n = 15), 2 indicated that others should take action (n = 31), 3 indicated awareness raising (n = 11), 4 indicated individual action (n = 9), and 5 indicated collective action (n = 24).
Notably, 46 participants (51.11%) reported a willingness to take action, suggesting a potential overreporting of action intentions compared to findings from general surveys (OECD, 2024).

To test our hypotheses, we fitted three linear mixed-effects models (MLMs) examining the effects of state of change (status quo vs. social change; Level 1) on cardiovascular challenge-threat responses (CO, TPR, and TCI), while accounting for repeated observations nested within participants (Level 2).

Models were estimated using maximum likelihood (ML; REML = FALSE) in R using the lme4 package (version 1.1-37; Bates et al., 2015) and included participant-specific random intercepts to account for the dependence among repeated observations.
text.formatted: Models were estimated using maximum likelihood (ML; REML = FALSE) in R using the lme4 package (version 1.1-37; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bates et al., 2015)</ref> and included participant-specific random intercepts to account for the dependence among repeated observations.

text.text: Random slopes were not estimated because each participant contributed only two observations.
Following the default specification in lme4, level-1 residuals were assumed to be independent and homoscedastic, with a common residual variance estimated across observations.

To examine whether threat also emerges among supporters of change, we sequentially added main and moderation effects between state of change and political orientation, eco-justice attitudes, neoliberalism attitudes, and speech-coded support.

Secondly, we planned to test whether the relationship between social change (vs. status quo) and threat and challenge responses was mediated by demands and resources using the multilevel mediation approach described by Bauer et al. (2006).
text.formatted: Secondly, we planned to test whether the relationship between social change (vs. status quo) and threat and challenge responses was mediated by demands and resources using the multilevel mediation approach described by <ref type="bibr">Bauer et al. (2006)</ref>.

text.text: This approach combines the mediator and dependent variable into a single stacked response variable and estimates all mediation paths within one mixed-effects model.
However, this analysis was not pursued further because the mediator did not significantly predict the outcome when included in the model.

To identify distinct participant profiles based on speech content and opinions on the academic boycott, we conducted a hierarchical cluster analysis (Ward's method, squared Euclidean distance) using z-scores of speech-coded support and demands, and resources.

The number of clusters was determined via agglomeration coefficients and dendrogram inspection from the hierarchical analysis, and the solution was refined using k-means clustering to optimize cluster membership.
We then ran one-way ANOVAs to test for differences in cardiac output (CO), total peripheral resistance (TPR), and Threat and Challenge Index (TCI) across clusters.

Finally, we explored whether physiological TCI and speech-coded support for social change predicted action intentions using logistic regressions, and whether clusters differed in terms of action intentions using X² tests.

We additionally examined whether cardiovascular challenge-threat responses varied as a function of the level of change manipulation (i.e., whether participants were instructed to focus their reflection on themselves, their ingroup, or the system) by adding the interaction between state of change and level of change to our previous models predicting CO, TPR, and TCI.

text.text: This shows that our speech paradigm was able to establish sufficient engagement for a further examination of CO and TPR in terms of threat and challenge.
Following these preliminary analyses, we tested our pre-registered Hypothesis 1 using multilevel models on baseline-adjusted physiological reactivity scores.
Unconditional mean models indicated substantial between-person variance for CO (ICC = .42), TPR (ICC = .47), and TCI (ICC = .44), supporting the use of multilevel modeling.

In line with our predictions, participants showed greater threat responses when speaking about the social change compared to the status quo, characterized by lower cardiac output (CO), β = -.67, 95% CI [-.85, -.49], p < .001 (Figure 1), higher total peripheral resistance (TPR), β = .44, 95% CI [.25, .63], p < .001 (Figure 2), and a lower threat-challenge index (TCI), β = -.61, 95% CI [-.79, -.43], p < .001 (Figure 3).

text.text: Across all three models, the random intercepts indicated substantial between-participant variability in starting levels of cardiovascular responses.
The estimated standard deviations of the random intercepts were 0.73 for CO, 0.72 for TPR, and 0.72 for TCI.
The estimated residual standard deviations were 0.59 for CO, 0.65 for TPR, and 0.61 for TCI.
Visual inspection of residual and Q-Q plots indicated no substantial violations of the assumptions of normality or homoscedasticity for any of the models.

Across Figures 1 2 3, a consistent pattern emerges: on average, participants showed a relative tendency towards physiological challenge responses during the status quo speech.

text.text: In contrast, average scores during the social change speech shifted toward a more threat response.
To be noted, however, individual responses varied in both conditions, with some participants exhibiting challenge responses and others showing threat responses regardless of the speech condition.

Descriptively, participants were, on average, moderately left-leaning (M = 5.00, SD = 1.18, on a 7-point scale), reported relatively positive eco-justice attitudes (M = 5.01, SD = 1.06), and expressed moderate opposition to neoliberal capitalism (M = 3.52, SD = 0.86).

Mixedmodel effects further revealed that participants expressed stronger support for the academic boycott (M = 5.40, SD = 1.46) than for the status quo (M = 3.19, SD = 1.18), β = 1.35, 95% CI [1.13, 1.58], p < .001.

text.text: To test whether social change elicited threat even among its supporters, we examined whether the effects of state of change on CO, TPR, and TCI were moderated by political orientation, eco-justice attitudes, neoliberal capitalism attitudes, and expressed support for social change.
Multilevel models included the corresponding main effects and their interactions with state.
Across all outcomes, state of change remained a significant predictor of lower CO and TCI, and higher TPR (all ps < .001).
text.formatted: Across all outcomes, state of change remained a significant predictor of lower CO and TCI, and higher TPR (all ps < .001).

text.text: Importantly, none of the interaction terms reached statistical significance (all ps ≥ .18), suggesting that the threatening effect of social change also persisted among its supporters.

We nonetheless observed an association between neoliberal capitalism attitudes and cardiovascular responses, such that stronger endorsement of neoliberal capitalism was associated with higher challenge, including higher CO (β = .21, 95% CI [-.01, .44], p = .062), lower TPR (β = -.21, 95% CI [-.44, .02], p = .075), and higher TCI (β = .23, 95% CI [.01, .46], p = .043), suggesting that participants with more progressive economic attitudes actually experienced higher threat than their less progressive counterparts.

These findings revealed a striking tendency: At an explicit level, people were more positive about social change than about the status quo; however, at an implicit, cardiovascular, level people were more threatened when reflecting on social change than on the status quo, somewhat regardless of their political orientation, their attitudes toward political issues, and their expressed support of social change.
Contrary to our Hypothesis 2, we did not find that survey demands and resources mediated the relationship between state of change and TCI (see Supplementary Material
Chapter 3, section 6 for details).

Somewhat in line with BPS-CT prediction and research (Seery, 2013), higher ingroup uncertainty correlated with a lower TCI (r = -.25; p = .018), suggesting that when a participant perceived their ingroup facing more uncertainties they may experience higher threat.

text.text: To further examine Hypothesis 2 and shed light on the different experiences people may have had when reflecting on social change, we then examined possible clusters based on speech-coded support for social change, demands, and resources.
Hierarchical cluster analysis suggested that either a 3-or 4-cluster solution could be justified.

Although the 3-cluster solution corresponded to a substantial increase in linkage distance around a rescaled distance of approximately 20-25, the 4-cluster solution identified at a slightly lower level, around 15-18, and allowed for greater differentiation among subgroups while still maintaining reasonable between-cluster separation.
Thus, a 4-cluster solution was preferred.
Such clusters are described below in order of support for social change, ranging from the most negative to the most positive.
We report cluster averages and standard deviations for the demands and resources measures.
All values should be interpreted relative to each measure's scale, so that labels such as "high" or "moderate" indicate levels within the context of that variable, rather than absolute magnitudes.

Interestingly, results from three one-way ANOVAs showed no significant differences between clusters in ecojustice attitudes (p = .511), neoliberalism attitudes (p = .061), or political orientation (p = .192).

Participants in this cluster (n = 11) showed opposition to the selective collaboration model (M = 2.64; SD = 1.21), paired with the highest use of rationalizations as resources (M = 1.82; SD = 0.60), and some value-interest conflict as a demand (M = 1.09; SD = 0.83).

These patterns suggest that, rather than openly expressing opposition, participants whose responses fell in this cluster tried to rationalize or justify their stance, and at times to defend a moral selfimage.

Participants in this cluster (n = 21) showed moderate support for the selective collaboration model (M = 4.67; SD = 0.86), paired with high status loss (M = 1.90: SD = 0.77), and value-interest conflict (M = 1.05; SD = 0.97), but low resources across all types.
Participants in this cluster appeared to struggle with the tension between maintaining a progressive moral image and confronting the real consequences implied by social change.

Participants in this cluster (N = 44) showed high support for the selective collaboration model (M = 6.14; SD = 0.71), paired with the strongest moral compass (M = 2.77: SD = 1.05), high moral support (M = 1.02; SD = 1.05), and some implementation concerns (M = 0.89; SD = 1.28).
Participants in this cluster were concerned about whether social change will achieve its intended outcomes, but they reaffirmed their support by appealing to moral reasoning and reframing of demands.

Participants in this cluster (N = 14) showed the highest support for the selective collaboration model (M = 6.36; SD = 0.74), paired with the highest instrumental support (M = 1.50: SD = 0.65), high moral support (M = 1.00; SD = 0.88), and mid-low demands across all types.
Participants in this cluster appear less concerned about the negative consequences of social change, while feeling supported and protected by the institutions and communities around them.
One-way ANOVAs showed significant differences on the threat-challenge index (TCI) among the four clusters, F(3, 85) = 10.43, p < .001, η² = 0.27 (Figure 4).

Rationalizing opponents (M = 0.05, SD = 1.23) exhibited a mild challenge response, while concerned moralists (M = -0.57, SD = 1.07) showed a mild threat response, with both clusters displaying relatively balanced distributions across threat and challenge categories.
These two clusters did not differ significantly from one another (d = -1.56, p = .582).

Logistic regression results showed that neither TCI (β = .188, p = .212) nor speechcoded support for change (β = .0.86, p = .512) significantly predicted action intentions.
In an exploratory manner, we then tested differences in action intentions among the four clusters (Figure 5).

text.text: Collective resilients tended to report more collective action intentions (n = 7, 70%), whereas rationalizing opponents slightly favored individual action (n = 3, 30%).
Concerned moralists appeared to lean toward collective action (n = 10, 37%) or indicated that others should act (n = 17, 63%).
Ambivalent supporters were somewhat more likely to indicate no action (n = 7, 30%) or that others should act (n = 10, 43%).
Importantly, although certain trends were observable, each cluster exhibited a variety of action types, indicating that these results are only indicative and not conclusive.
This is further underscored by the uneven cluster sizes, which ranged from small (11) to large (44).
Proportion of Action Type per Cluster of Speech-coded Support, Demands, and Resources

In the current research, we investigated whether systemic and progressive social change, in the form of an academic boycott of unsustainable and unethical collaboration partners, elicited a physiological threat response, even among supporters of change.
To assess this, we tested whether the threat response persisted after controlling for the main and moderating effect of political orientation and survey and speech-coded attitudes toward change.
We additionally explored potential root causes of such threat responses, by looking at scale and speech-coded demands and resources, and whether physiological responses influenced action intentions.

In line with our pre-registered Hypothesis 1 we found that, compared to the status quo, participants in the social change condition displayed lower Cardiac Output (CO), increased Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR), and relatively low scores on a combined Threat and Challenge Index (TCI).
All these results indicate a clear threat response to social change in the form of an academic boycott-like initiative targeting unsustainable and unethical collaborations.
These were not moderated by political orientation and attitudes toward change and persisted when controlling for these variables.
Importantly, participants expressed stronger support for social change compared to the status quo, suggesting a possible tension between expressed support and cardiovascular responses.
Contrary to Hypothesis 2, neither survey demands, nor survey resources predicted cardiovascular threat or challenge responses.

Interestingly, however, we still found an association between increased perceived ingroup uncertainty and physiological threat, suggesting that the extent to which participants felt uncertain about their (academic) ingroup may be associated with physiological threat responses, in line with BPS-CT predictions.
Finally, neither threat nor challenge responses, nor expressed support for social change, directly predicted action intentions measured through an open-ended question.

Exploratory analyses tentatively suggested meaningful cluster differences: threatened clusters (ambivalent supporters and concerned moralists) tended toward inaction and delegation of responsibility, although concerned moralists expressed some collective action intentions; collective resilients reported more collective action intentions, whereas rationalizing showed action intentions comparable to concerned moralists without however delegating to others.
These patterns should be interpreted as indicative rather than conclusive.

Our findings provided initial empirical support for extending the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Blascovich & Mendes, 2010) into the domain of hierarchy-disruptive social change.
text.formatted: Our findings provided initial empirical support for extending the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref> into the domain of hierarchy-disruptive social change.

text.text: Participants displayed prototypical threat physiology, namely lower cardiac output (CO) combined with increased total peripheral resistance (TPR), when reflecting on social change initiatives, and even when controlling for their political orientation, attitudes, and expressed support for the change.
This tension between expressed support and physiological responses aligns with Seery's (2013) observation that subjective measures often fail to capture underlying motivational states.
text.formatted: This tension between expressed support and physiological responses aligns with <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery's (2013)</ref> observation that subjective measures often fail to capture underlying motivational states.

text.text: By integrating cardiovascular markers, we revealed hidden stress responses patterns that might have remained invisible using survey measures alone (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: By integrating cardiovascular markers, we revealed hidden stress responses patterns that might have remained invisible using survey measures alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: It further suggests that the threat posed by social change may persist even among those who support it.

This may raise the possibility that responses to such changes depend not only on individuals' support for the change itself, but also on how they appraise the demands it creates relative to the resources they perceive as available to cope with them, as suggested by our cluster analyses and, to a lesser extent, our survey measures.
It should be noted that the survey, text, and physiological indices of challenge and threat differed in the precise targets of their appraisals, despite their relation to each other.

That is, in the survey and text coding, demands and resources referred to an evaluation of the two respective collaboration models, while the physiological measures most directly refer to challenge and threat in the motivated performance situation, i.e., forming and expressing one's opinion on the two collaboration models.

Still, we propose that these different appraisals, captured through self-reports and reflected in physiological measures of challenge and threat, were meaningfully related, as was suggested from the cluster analysis.
Indeed, speech content could be in a meaningful way related to demands (e.g., uncertainty, required effort) and resources (e.g., support) described by the BPS-CT.

For example, uncertainty is an inherent aspect of social change and can operate as a negative "affective cue" (Blascovich & Mendes, 2000) feeding into a physiological threat response when reflecting on, and responding to, change.
text.formatted: For example, uncertainty is an inherent aspect of social change and can operate as a negative "affective cue" <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2000)</ref> feeding into a physiological threat response when reflecting on, and responding to, change.

text.text: Moreover, ambivalent and rationalizing responses to social change may have been demanding because they required more effort than reflecting on the status quo.

Finally, at the resource side of the appraisal part of the BPS-CT, feeling supported, i.e., knowing that one is not alone in one's opinion, may have fed into the relative challenge response among collective resilients.

Overall, we propose that a blend of different demand and resource factors, at different levels of analysis, possibly contributed to the physiological threat responses to social change, as well as to the substantial variation in this response as evident from the cluster analysis.
Indeed, it seems unlikely that the threat of social change as observed here would have been due to a single factor.

For example, although required effort is likely to have been a central demand, if this would have been the only factor, one would have also expected stronger signs of engagement (HR, PEP) than were currently observed in the social change condition (see also Gendolla & Richter, 2010; Wright & Kirby, 2001).
text.formatted: For example, although required effort is likely to have been a central demand, if this would have been the only factor, one would have also expected stronger signs of engagement (HR, PEP) than were currently observed in the social change condition (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Gendolla & Richter, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wright & Kirby, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Still, despite that, a strong case can be made for the connection between the broader demands and resources of social change and the more specific demands and resources when expressing one's opinion on the change.
We also note that future research should connect demands and resources at different levels of analysis of (the threat of) social change even more directly and explicitly than we were able to do here.

Notably, although meaningful differences in cardiovascular challenge and threat emerged across clusters characterized by distinct patterns of expressed demands and resources, survey-measures demands and resources did not mediate the relationship between state of change and cardiovascular responses.
This suggests that the mechanisms underlying these physiological responses are only partially captured in our study.
One explanation is methodological, as self-reports were collected after the speech task whereas cardiovascular responses were recorded during it, allowing for possible shifts over time.
Alternatively, cardiovascular challenge and threat may reflect rapid or partially nonconscious appraisals not fully captured by retrospective self-report (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: Alternatively, cardiovascular challenge and threat may reflect rapid or partially nonconscious appraisals not fully captured by retrospective self-report <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings align with theoretical insight proposing that hierarchy-disruptive social changes are often experienced as stressful and destabilizing (De La Sablonnière, 2017) and, consistent with the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat (BPS-CT; Seery, 2014), they can elicit physiological threat responses.

Prior research has shown that challenges to traditional norms, hierarchical structures, or exposure to minoritized group members are particularly status-threatening for dominant group members and conservatives, resulting in heightened physiological stress (Long et al., 2025; Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018; Scheepers & Knight, 2020).
text.formatted: Prior research has shown that challenges to traditional norms, hierarchical structures, or exposure to minoritized group members are particularly status-threatening for dominant group members and conservatives, resulting in heightened physiological stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Long et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Scheepers & Knight, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Extending this literature, the present study suggests that even individuals who outwardly support progressive social change can exhibit physiological signs of threat, maybe especially when their own or their ingroup's privileges or resources are perceived to be at risk, or when uncertainties and concerns arise regarding the implementation of social change.

This divergence from previous work may reflect our focus on systemic, ecologically grounded social movement-driven changes, rather than the more constrained intergroup competition paradigms commonly used in prior research.

By situating participants within realistic scenarios of broad societal transformation, our approach may have enabled them to engage more directly with the complex material implications and tensions inherent in hierarchy-disruptive social change, making the demands and uncertainties associated with these changes salient even for those who supported them.
Our cluster analyses provide some tentative insight into why supporters may experience such threat.

One possible explanation concerns potential losses to personal or ingroup privileges, together with tensions between endorsing social justice in principle and fearing the implications of change, as seen among ambivalent supporters.

The uncertainty stemming from this tension may help explain their heightened threat responses (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010), as suggested also by the link found between survey-measured ingroup uncertainty and TCI.
text.formatted: The uncertainty stemming from this tension may help explain their heightened threat responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>, as suggested also by the link found between survey-measured ingroup uncertainty and TCI.

text.text: This pattern aligns with Tosaka's (2024) argument that liberals who endorse justice in principle may nonetheless resist systemic interventions when those interventions require personal or group sacrifice.
text.formatted: This pattern aligns with <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Tosaka's (2024)</ref> argument that liberals who endorse justice in principle may nonetheless resist systemic interventions when those interventions require personal or group sacrifice.

text.text: It also resonates with the notion of performative allyship (Kutlaca & Radke, 2022), and the evidence gathered about the attitude-implementation gap (Glasford, 2022), wherein symbolic support fails to translate into substantive action.
text.formatted: It also resonates with the notion of performative allyship <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Kutlaca & Radke, 2022)</ref>, and the evidence gathered about the attitude-implementation gap <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Glasford, 2022)</ref>, wherein symbolic support fails to translate into substantive action.

text.text: Our findings suggest that this gap may at times be driven by an unresolved conflict between endorsing abstract values and confronting the costly realities of progress.

Regardless of intentions, vague ideals could prove hollow, potentially contributing to the delegation of responsibility to others, which may give the appearance of progress while leaving the status quo largely intact.
Threat, although lower, was also observed among concerned moralists, who tended to frame potential losses as moral imperatives.
Unlike the vague ideals observed in ambivalent supporters, these moral imperatives were more concrete and were accompanied by greater acceptance of the costly reality of progress.
This more concrete framing may partly account for the presence of some collective action intentions among this cluster, alongside delegating responsibility to others.

While these findings are tentative, they are broadly consistent with the idea that moral obligation, rooted in deeply shared values, strongly motivates collective action (Ellemers et al., 2019; Sabucedo et al., 2018; Uysal et al., 2022).
text.formatted: While these findings are tentative, they are broadly consistent with the idea that moral obligation, rooted in deeply shared values, strongly motivates collective action <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Ellemers et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Sabucedo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Uysal et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Related research on utopian thinking likewise showed that envisioning more just futures can elicit hope, reduce system justification, and strengthen intentions to act (Badaan et al., 2022; Badaan et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Related research on utopian thinking likewise showed that envisioning more just futures can elicit hope, reduce system justification, and strengthen intentions to act <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Badaan et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Badaan et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, although moral imperatives seem more motivating than vague ideals, they may still be insufficient to drive sustained collective action, bringing further nuance to previous work on the role of morality in social change.

Taken together, our cluster analyses suggest that individuals may occupy intermediate psychological positions during periods of systemic change, simultaneously supporting progressive reforms while experiencing threat arising from anticipated losses, uncertainty, and competing values.
Although these findings remain preliminary, they suggest the possibility that threat may not simply distinguish supporters from opponents of hierarchy-disruptive social change.
Rather, it may represent a partially common, though different in content, response to the demands of systemic change, even among those who ultimately endorse it.
Our findings may also suggest that the implications of threat may depend on how it is navigated.

While ambivalent supporters appeared to remain caught between abstract commitments to justice and concerns about the costs of change, concerned moralists likewise exhibited physiological threat but were more likely to frame those costs as morally necessary and expressed at least some willingness to engage in collective action.
This pattern suggests that experiencing threat need not always be incompatible with supporting or acting toward social change.
Threat may not be interpreted as inherently and absolutely negative (or positive).

Rather than something to be avoided in the interest of social harmony (Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018), it may represent a recurring feature of systemic change (de la Sablonnière, 2017), with downstream consequences that depend on whether individuals can integrate perceived losses and uncertainties into a meaningful commitment to change.
text.formatted: Rather than something to be avoided in the interest of social harmony <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Scheepers & Ellemers, 2018)</ref>, it may represent a recurring feature of systemic change (de la Sablonnière, 2017), with downstream consequences that depend on whether individuals can integrate perceived losses and uncertainties into a meaningful commitment to change.

text.text: This interpretation aligns with emerging evidence that negative affect is not inherently maladaptive.
For example, downregulating negative emotions during daily political engagement may improve well-being but reduce collective action intentions (Ford et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, downregulating negative emotions during daily political engagement may improve well-being but reduce collective action intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ford et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, perceived ingroup threat can motivate action through heightened injustice appraisals and identification (Szóstakowski & Besta, 2024), while framing collective trauma as a challenge has been linked to greater mobilization (Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Likewise, perceived ingroup threat can motivate action through heightened injustice appraisals and identification <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Szóstakowski & Besta, 2024)</ref>, while framing collective trauma as a challenge has been linked to greater mobilization <ref type="bibr">(Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, the BPS-CT framework suggests that experiencing elements of both threat and challenge may facilitate adaptive coping by promoting flexibility and sustained effort (Uphill et al., 2019).
text.formatted: More broadly, the BPS-CT framework suggests that experiencing elements of both threat and challenge may facilitate adaptive coping by promoting flexibility and sustained effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Uphill et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Although no research has yet directly examined how initial threat during hierarchydisruptive social change may evolve into challenge over time, our findings suggest this transition may represent a promising avenue for future research.

Future research could track physiological threat and challenge at multiple stages, such as during an initial speech and after reflection, to examine how initial responses evolve and identify conditions that promote adaptive, challenge-oriented engagement.

Importantly, this possibility does not minimize the potentially detrimental effects of early threat responses, such as withdrawal, poorer performance and especially detrimental effects on well-being and physical health.

This is tentatively suggested by the observation that among concerned moralists, and even more so among ambivalent supporters, many reported that others should take action for change, and some that no action should be taken, consistent with BPS-CT linking threat to withdrawal.
Observations from the collective resilients clusters may suggest how threat could move toward challenge, possibly over time.

In particular, collective resources, including trust in collective capacity, some forms of institutional support, and shared responsibility expressed by collective resilients, could play a role in this process, as also shown in research linking perceived collective efficacy to greater engagement in collective action (Bandura, 2000; Lucarini et al., 2025; Uysal et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In particular, collective resources, including trust in collective capacity, some forms of institutional support, and shared responsibility expressed by collective resilients, could play a role in this process, as also shown in research linking perceived collective efficacy to greater engagement in collective action <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bandura, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Lucarini et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Uysal et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although support has been identified as a key resource (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010), BPS-CT research has primarily focused on individuals' appraisals of their own demands and coping resources.
text.formatted: Although support has been identified as a key resource <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010)</ref>, BPS-CT research has primarily focused on individuals' appraisals of their own demands and coping resources.

text.text: The present findings suggest that future research should also investigate the role of collective resources in supporting more adaptive responses to hierarchy-disruptive social change.
A key contribution of our study is its grounding in a real-world context: an academic boycott campaign.

Political boycotts, often initiated by minorities or marginalized groups seeking to challenge entrenched power structures, have a long and effective history within social movements, from their central role in the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa to their influence on climate-justice initiatives and contemporary mobilizations for Palestinian rights (Ayling & Gunningham, 2017; Barghouti, 2011).
text.formatted: Political boycotts, often initiated by minorities or marginalized groups seeking to challenge entrenched power structures, have a long and effective history within social movements, from their central role in the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa to their influence on climate-justice initiatives and contemporary mobilizations for Palestinian rights <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ayling & Gunningham, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Barghouti, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Traditional research often operationalizes social change in abstract, depoliticized terms that reflect majority-centered interests (e.g., societal harmony, inclusivity), potentially overlooking the high stakes and emotional tensions inherent in minority-centered social change (e.g., land protection, economic restructuring) (see Becker, 1967).
text.formatted: Traditional research often operationalizes social change in abstract, depoliticized terms that reflect majority-centered interests (e.g., societal harmony, inclusivity), potentially overlooking the high stakes and emotional tensions inherent in minority-centered social change (e.g., land protection, economic restructuring) (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Becker, 1967)</ref>.

text.text: Reviewing previous physiological research, we noticed a mismatch between studies relying on hypothetical scenarios and those engaging participants with more realistic change contexts.

Recent work by Bacchini et al. (2024), including four studies using both self-report and psychophysiological measures, shows that when social change (versus stability) is made salient in the form of discussing gender norms, dominant group members (e.g., men) often experience less distress and fewer negative self-focused emotions, which ironically reduces their willingness to engage in collective action.
text.formatted: Recent work by <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bacchini et al. (2024)</ref>, including four studies using both self-report and psychophysiological measures, shows that when social change (versus stability) is made salient in the form of discussing gender norms, dominant group members (e.g., men) often experience less distress and fewer negative self-focused emotions, which ironically reduces their willingness to engage in collective action.

text.text: This seems to align with what we observed in our rationalizing opponent cluster, whose members exhibited mild cardiovascular challenge while expressing opposition to social change and rationalizations.
Moreover, physiological data from webcam-based heart rate monitoring revealed lower engagement under social change compared to stability, even as participants reported relatively positive attitudes.
This divergence suggests that explicit openness to change may coexist with an implicitly measured lack of engagement, raising doubts about whether stated support would translate into action.

We propose that this abstract intergroup (majority-centered) versus concrete politicized (minority-centered) framing of social change masks one of the points at which support ambivalence emerges: when social change is grounded in the practice of social movements and objectives of marginalized communities, as in the case of the present study, it may become more difficult for some supporters to maintain abstract endorsement without confronting the personal and structural implications of change, some of which they may not ultimately endorse in their more material aspects, or are less able to cope with.
While the present study offers novel insights into physiological responses to progressive social change, several limitations should be acknowledged.
A first limitation concerns the absence of counterbalancing in the order of the two conditions of state of change.
This departs from standard experimental practice, where randomization is typically used to disentangle condition effects from potential order effects, and therefore represents a potential confound.

At the same time, if order effects were driving the findings, one would typically expect a more uniform reduction in physiological engagement and in challenge-threat responses consistent with habituation (Hughes et al. 2018).
text.formatted: At the same time, if order effects were driving the findings, one would typically expect a more uniform reduction in physiological engagement and in challenge-threat responses consistent with habituation <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Hughes et al. 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Instead, while participants showed lower physiological engagement during the second speech, their physiological responses also shifted from challenge to threat, alongside higher self-reported challenge, and increased perceptions of both demands and resources.

Moreover, as described in the https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd (section 6), even though engagement seemed lower during the second speech task, the results on challenge and threat relevant cardiovascular activity hold when controlling for physiological markers of task engagement (i.e., HR, PEP reactivity).
text.formatted: Moreover, as described in the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hnf8b/overview?view_only=0be6dbcb31b14394a731fc47e99577bd">Supplementary Materials Chapter 3</ref> (section 6), even though engagement seemed lower during the second speech task, the results on challenge and threat relevant cardiovascular activity hold when controlling for physiological markers of task engagement (i.e., HR, PEP reactivity).

text.text: Given the brief and low-burden nature of the tasks (a 300-word reading and a 1minute speech), a fatigue-based explanation also appears unlikely to fully account for these effects.
This pattern is therefore more consistent with a threat response to social change than with a generic order effect, although we acknowledge that it cannot be fully ruled out.

This design choice was further guided by theoretical and ecological considerations (de la Sablonnière, 2017), according to which social change is inherently evaluated relative to a stable baseline (i.e., the status quo), which serves as a necessary reference point and increased the ecological validity of our findings.
Future research should nevertheless replicate these findings using counterbalanced designs to more fully address potential order-related confounds.
Furthermore, our operationalization of demands and resources relied on self-report measures that were relatively broad, capturing general perceptions of effort, uncertainty, and support.

These measures did not significantly mediate physiological threat responses, likely because they were collected post-task and may have reflected reflective rationalizations rather than real-time appraisals (Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: These measures did not significantly mediate physiological threat responses, likely because they were collected post-task and may have reflected reflective rationalizations rather than real-time appraisals <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Future research could benefit from developing more fine-grained, quantitative measures of demands and resources, and potentially aligning with the thematic categories that we identified in participants' speeches.

For instance, participants could rate the anticipated impact of a social change on specific domains, such as career opportunities, financial stability, moral integrity, collective efficacy, which may more closely capture the real-time trade-offs that drive physiological threat or challenge responses (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2013).
text.formatted: For instance, participants could rate the anticipated impact of a social change on specific domains, such as career opportunities, financial stability, moral integrity, collective efficacy, which may more closely capture the real-time trade-offs that drive physiological threat or challenge responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Seery, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, while this study provides valuable insight into how people navigate tensions toward progress and action, it relies largely on qualitative and exploratory analyses.

This approach was necessary to access the kinds of conflicts people actually experience (see Dixon et al., 2017), which may be difficult to detect in survey responses that are shaped by socialdesirability concerns or constrained by predefined items.
text.formatted: This approach was necessary to access the kinds of conflicts people actually experience (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Dixon et al., 2017)</ref>, which may be difficult to detect in survey responses that are shaped by socialdesirability concerns or constrained by predefined items.

text.text: Moreover, because BPS-CT offers relatively limited theorizing on how physiological appraisals operate in real-world systemic sociopolitical contexts, our analyses were necessarily exploratory.
Future research could build on these initial observations with more quantitative and hypothesis-driven designs.
Building on our results, future research could examine differences between dominant and minoritized group members in relation to support of social change, within the BPS-CT framework.
Although prior work has distinguished between these groups, it has rarely done so in the context of systemic progressive social change.

Given that minoritized communities are often at the forefront of movements driving such change, understanding whether and why threat responses arise, and how they can be navigated constructively, remains an important direction for further work, both practically and theoretically, in addition to understanding such responses among supporters.
Relatedly, as noted above, it would be valuable to investigate how threat and challenge appraisals unfold over time.

Longitudinal designs could clarify whether and how an initial threat response can evolve into a challenge response as individuals mobilize collective resources, reframe status losses, and cope with the uncertainties inherent to progressive hierarchy-disruptive social change.
Across Western liberal democracies, structural violence and individual inaction persist beneath a veneer of progressivism.
Although research on the attitude-implementation gap and collective action has documented this contradiction, the motivational (physiological) processes underlying it remain unclear.

Drawing on the BPS-CT framework, our findings showed that physiological threat responses to systemic change, here an academic boycott-like initiative, can emerge even when individuals express support.
Importantly, these responses were not uniform.

For some participants, threat appeared rooted in unwillingness to relinquish privileges and difficulty reconciling them with abstract progressive values, accompanied by reluctance to act and a tendency to shift responsibility.

For others, threat reflected awareness of the discomfort and sacrifice required to pursue meaningful systemic change, paired with mixed responses, both intentions to act and impulses to delegate responsibility.

This distinction offers a more nuanced and constructive view of threat: because progressive change is inherently destabilizing, the capacity to engage with and regulate initial responses may help foster more sustained, challenge-oriented action over time.
These results extend prior BPS-CT work, which has largely emphasized threat avoidance.
Instead, our study hints at the value of confronting, rather than bypassing, the tensions of hierarchy-disruptive social change.

Figure3 examining Hypothesis 2, analysis of speech-coded support for social change, demands, and resources regarding the selective collaboration model identified four distinct participant profiles.

Ambivalent supporters (highest threat responses, struggling to reconcile progressive values with the perceived costs and challenges of social change); concerned moralists (milder threat responses, acknowledging the losses associated with change while reaffirming personal and collective moral commitments to it); rationalizing opponents (mild challenge responses, justifying their opposition to change); collective resilients (strongest challenge responses, expressing moral and material collective resources alongside low demands).
Noticeably, collective demands and resources, such as ingroup uncertainty and losses and shared responsibilities, appeared to exert the strongest influence on participants' responses.

However, our manipulation of level of change did not work as intended (see Supplementary Materials Chapter 3, section 7), underscoring the need for future research on how personal, ingroup, and system levels of change shape threat and challenge.
